In yesterday's post I included an inaccurate image. The image had cross sections of a shield volcano and a stratovolcano both sitting side by side on continental crust. If this image were accurate, the shield volcano would be on oceanic crust, and the stratovolcano would be on continental crust.

So magma/lava is hot. When it comes into contact with solid rock it tends to cook the rocks around it, and also it causes them to melt or partially melt in what is known as a "baked zone". Oceanic crust is primarily basalt and gabbro, which is what "pure" lava/magma is made of. It's the kind of rock that has low viscosity when it is melted. When a magma chamber forms in basalts and gabbros, the melt from the surrounding rock mixes with the magma, and doesn't change the chemical composition much. When this happens in continental crust (which is felsic if you'll recall) the silicone and feldspar melt down and join the magma. This gums up the magma, making it thicker and more resistant to flow (viscous). Not only this but a lot of gasses are released which are then mixed in with the magma. I tend to think of this magma like really hot carbonated maple syrup.

This is the kind of magma that forms under stratovolcanoes. The most famous stratovolcano (at least for the US) is probably Mount Saint Hellens. Here is a video of a stratovolcano eruption: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lIjaxltKaoE. Just to see the difference, here is a shield volcano eruption video that I should have posted in the last update:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HOV0AQHeE7Q (the good part starts around 40 minutes 45 seconds into the video).

See the difference? That's the difference that dissolved gasses and silicone make when the pressure is released. Generally, the stratovolcano is like opening a bottle of soda, where a shield volcanoe is like opening a bottle of water.

Bonus info: If you look back at my post on igneous rock classification the magmas in stratovolcanoes are rhyolitic/granitic to dioritic/andesitic (felsic magmas), while shield volcanoes are basaltic/gabbritic magmas (mafic magmas).

I'll probably end up doing a post on the details of Mount Saint Hellens eruption soon, because the details of the eruption are really cool and terrifying.
